newsitem.title: USA: Republicans pressed to back chemical weapons pact.
newsitem.headline: Republicans pressed to back chemical weapons pact.

text.p: Republicans will bear the responsibility if the Senate does not approve the Chemical Weapons Convention this week, Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle said on Monday.

The treaty to outlaw chemical weapons needs 67 votes in the 100-member Senate, a two-thirds majority, for approval. All 45 Democrats are expected to support it but the chances of getting the remaining votes from the 55 Republicans are seen as no better than even.

"It all comes down to whether or not there are 22 Republicans who are willing to provide the necessary votes," Daschle, of South Dakota, told reporters. The House of Representatives is not required to take action on the treaty.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said on Sunday he had concerns about provisions in the treaty and had not decided how he would vote. North Carolina Republican Jesse Helms, the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and some other conservative Republicans are strongly opposed to it.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Monday that President Bill Clinton would be "very active" in lobbying for the treaty prior to Thursday's Senate vote. He said Clinton made a round of telephone calls to senators on Saturday.
"He's making progress, but we're not there yet," he said.

The treaty was signed in 1993 and has been ratified by more than 70 countries. It takes effect on April 29, with or without U.S. approval. Russia, Iran and Iraq are among the other nations that have not ratified the treaty.

Daschle, making clear he placed the onus on Republicans for getting the treaty approved, said: "The Republican Caucus is going to have to decide whether it wants to be part of the international community or whether it wants to avoid ... taking on the initiatives necessary to ensure that we can continue to play the role of superpower for the world."

The pact was negotiated under Republican Presidents Ronald Reagan and George Bush. Submitted to the Senate by Clinton in November 1993, it languished until last September when it was brought up for debate, only to be withdrawn when Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole opposed it.

Debate is scheduled to start on Wednesday. Before the final vote on Thursday, the Senate will vote on five amendments that supporters say would kill U.S. participation in the convention if any were approved. They would:
-- bar U.S. participation in the treaty until Russia ratifies it and complies with an earlier agreement to destroy its poison gas stocks;
-- block U.S. ratification until "rogue states," such as Iraq and Libya sign on;
-- strike out treaty provisions that would require exchange of information between countries, including information on protection against chemical weapons;
-- raise standards for verification against cheating, including requiring the ability to detect as little as one metric ton of a chemical weapons agent;
-- bar inspectors from U.S. chemical facilities under the treaty if they were nationals of states designated by Washington as supporters of international terrorism.
